story.title: The website that wasn't integrated
story.context: A mid-sized retailer hires an agency to build a new e-commerce website.
story.agreed: New e-commerce website, delivered in four months.
story.client_private: It will end the manual order handling their team does.
story.agency_private: A clean storefront sitting on the existing back office.
story.unknowns: Integration with the stock system, with no owner, no scope and no budget. The word integration was never said.

story.signal: The client describes outcomes, such as less manual work, while the agency describes outputs, such as pages and a checkout.

agency.project: We're building a new e-commerce website for a mid-sized retailer, and the plan is to have it delivered in four months. That's the headline of what we've agreed so far.

turns.question: For the four months you've planned, how many rounds of feedback does your plan assume, and what happens once those are used up?
turns.answer: We've assumed two rounds of consolidated feedback on design and one on the built site, with the client giving us one set of comments per round. Once those are used, further changes are handled as change requests and quoted separately, though I'll admit we haven't spelled that out in detail with them yet.
turns.rationale: Taken from the agency persona agent. No conflicts exist yet, so rule 1 does not apply. Rule 2 applies: its priority 1 question on feedback rounds is the highest-priority question on a topic still missing for the agency side. Nothing has been asked of this person yet, so no repeat limit applies. I kept the wording to what the person has said (website, four months) and did not mention anything from the client side.

turns.answer: I see the price as covering design, build, testing and launch of the storefront. I'd treat licences, hosting, payment provider fees and photography as the client's own costs. I don't think we've said that to them in so many words yet, so it's an assumption on my side.
turns.rationale: Taken from ops. No fundamental or workable conflicts are reported, so rule 2 applies: ops has the priority 1 question on a missing topic (price inclusions and exclusions). Agency has already been asked twice in a row at most once so far, and ops has not yet been heard from. The client side has said nothing private that I need to touch here.

pending.rationale: Taken from the client persona agent. Rule 1 applies: there is a fundamental conflict, since the client expects manual order handling to stop and the agency has only described a storefront. The question is open and does not mention the client's order handling, so that stays private. The agency and ops agents have already been asked, so the client agent is the one this side has heard least from.

client.project: We're a mid-sized retailer and we've hired your agency to build us a new e-commerce website. The plan is to have it delivered in four months.

turns.question: What problem in your business are you hoping the new website will fix, and what should be different once it is live?
turns.answer: Mostly the manual order handling. My team spends a lot of time dealing with orders by hand, and once the new site is live I expect that to stop. Beyond that, I'd like a site that looks better and is easier for customers to use.
turns.rationale: Taken from the client persona agent. No conflicts exist, so rule 2 applies: its priority 1 question on the real goal, which is missing for this side. No persona agent has been asked yet, and this topic is the thinnest and underpins everything else.

turns.answer: Orders come in and my team retypes the details into our internal system, then sorts out the paperwork and passes them on to the warehouse. Once the new site is live, I expect orders to just go through without anyone handling them. I haven't mapped out the exact steps beyond that.
turns.rationale: Taken from the ops agent, which reports a fundamental conflict: the client expects the site to end manual order handling, which implies integration, while the agency has described only a website. Rule 1 applies, a fundamental conflict comes first. The client agent has already been used once, so ops is next, and the client's last answer opened exactly this topic.

story.title: The rebrand that wasn't brave enough
story.context: A brand hires an agency to refresh its identity for a new market.
story.agreed: Refresh the identity for a new market.
story.client_private: You are the marketing director. You need something bold enough to impress a new CEO in her first hundred days. You have not defined what brave means.
story.unknowns: The new CEO's expectations, never discussed with the agency.
story.intervention_question: If this lands perfectly, what does it let you say to your CEO, and what would make you say it wasn't enough?
story.signal: A goal that never appears in the brief but is hinted at with words like new market, fresh start or bold, used without definition.

agency.project: We're helping a brand refresh its identity so it works in a new market it's moving into. That's the scope on paper, and we're getting started on what that looks like in practice.

turns.question: When you picture the last day of this project, what will you have handed over, such as a logo, guidelines or templates, that someone could check off one by one?
turns.answer: I picture an evolved version of the logo, an adjusted color palette and typography, a brand guidelines document, and a starter set of templates for the main applications. The exact list isn't pinned down yet, so that's my working picture rather than something we've signed off.
turns.rationale: No conflicts reported by any persona agent, so rule 1 does not apply. Rule 2: priority 1 questions on missing topics exist from agency and ops; I chose the ops question on what is handed over on the last day, because 'refresh' is still undefined and the agency itself said 'what that looks like in practice' is open, so it follows their own words. Nothing from the client side is used, and no persona agent has been asked yet.

turns.question: What does your price cover for this work, and what would you count as extra if the client asked for it?
turns.answer: My price is meant to cover the evolved logo, the adjusted palette and typography, the guidelines document, and the starter templates, with a reasonable amount of revision along the way. I'd count as extra a ground-up redesign, extra templates or applications beyond the starter set, additional market research, and revision rounds past what we've allowed for. I haven't written that line down in detail yet, so it's still my working assumption.
turns.rationale: Took the question from ops (priority 1, price boundary missing). No fundamental or workable conflict is ready to probe directly without leaking the client's mention of how the brand sounds; the ops conflict on tone of voice is only unproven. Ops has been asked once so far, so a second in a row is allowed, and the price boundary is the biggest unowned gap.

pending.question: What do you think this brand is really trying to achieve in the new market, and how much visible change do you think that calls for?
pending.rationale: Taken from the client persona agent. Rule 1 applies: there is a fundamental conflict on scale of change, since the agency pictures an evolved logo and adjusted palette while the client wants something noticeably bolder, not a light tweak. The agency's own view of the real goal is still missing, so I'm asking it openly without hinting at what the client said, and I have already asked ops twice.

client.project: We're a brand heading into a new market, and we want to refresh our identity so it fits there. It's about updating how we look and sound so we come across well to a new audience.

turns.question: Once the refresh is done and you are up and running in the new market, what would be visibly different for your business that tells you it worked?
turns.answer: Honestly, I'd want it to feel noticeably bolder than what we have now, so that people in the new market take notice and it doesn't look like a light tweak of the old identity. I haven't pinned down what "bolder" means in practice, and I don't have a metric in mind yet.
turns.rationale: Taken from the client persona agent. No conflicts exist yet, so rule 2 applied: its priority 1 question on a missing topic (success you can point at). The goal is currently only a deliverable, so nobody could say yes or no to it at the end. The question uses only words the client has said: brand, new market, refresh.

turns.question: Can you think of a brand, or something you have seen, that you would call bold enough, and something that would feel too timid?
turns.answer: Off the top of my head, something like Liquid Death feels bold to me, because nobody could mistake it for anything else. Timid would be those rebrands where the logo gets a bit cleaner and a new color, and you'd struggle to spot the difference side by side. I'm reacting on instinct there, and I couldn't tell you yet how far we'd want to go.
turns.rationale: Taking the ops question (priority 1), since ops reports a fundamental conflict on what 'refresh' and 'done' mean, which comes first under the rules. The client has just admitted 'bolder' is undefined, so this follows what they opened up. The agency's 'evolved' and 'adjusted' wording is not mentioned to the client.

pending.question: Thinking about what you have now, which parts, such as the name, the logo shape, the colours or the way you sound, would you be happy to change completely, and which must stay?
pending.rationale: Taken from the agency persona's priority 1 question on how far the client will go. Rule 1 applies: the fundamental conflict over 'evolved' versus 'bolder' is the top issue, and the client has just said they cannot yet say how far they would go. Client persona questions have been asked, so this follows the new opening, and it avoids mentioning the agency's scope or price wording.

story.title: The portal that grew forty percent
story.context: A software agency builds a customer portal.
story.agreed: A defined portal scope, fixed budget.
story.client_private: Small requests along the way are covered by goodwill and will not cost extra.
story.agency_private: Say yes to each small request to keep the relationship friendly.
story.unknowns: Nobody owns a running total of changes, and neither side could see the cumulative size of them.
story.intervention_question: A running tally of changes against the original agreement, with a prompt at a set threshold, say ten percent growth, asking both sides to confirm they still agree the total is fine.
story.signal: Repeated small requests with no corresponding change to scope or budget.

agency.project: We're building a customer portal for them, with a defined scope and a fixed budget that we've both agreed on. It's a fairly standard piece of work for us, and we're keen to get it done well and keep things running smoothly.

turns.question: You mentioned a fixed budget and a defined scope, so how many rounds of feedback have you allowed for within that price?
turns.answer: We haven't put a specific number of feedback rounds on paper, as far as I recall. In practice I've been planning to just say yes to the small requests as they come up, to keep things friendly.
turns.rationale: No conflicts are flagged, so rule 1 does not apply. Rule 2 applies: priority 1 questions on missing topics exist from agency and ops. No persona agent has been used yet, so I took the agency persona's feedback rounds question, which is the biggest risk behind a fixed budget. I left out the client's own words and anything from the client side.

turns.question: When a small request comes in and you say yes, how do you plan to keep track of it so you both remember what was agreed?
turns.answer: I don't have a formal way of tracking them right now. I've mostly been agreeing in emails or calls and relying on memory, and I hadn't really thought about it until you asked.
turns.rationale: Took the question from ops. A workable conflict exists on change and scope: the agency plans informal yeses with no round limit, while the client reads the fixed price as the whole deal. Rule 1 says a conflict comes first, and the answer just opened this up, so I follow it. Ops asks who can request changes and how they get recorded, which I trimmed to one question using only the agency's own words.

pending.question: In your own words, what do you think they are hoping the portal will achieve for their customers?
pending.rationale: Took the question from the client persona agent. Already asked agency then ops, and the agency has had two in a row so the client agent is the one this side has heard least from. No fundamental conflict exists, only a workable risk on changes which the last two answers have covered, and the client agent's priority 1 goal and audience question is missing for this side. Phrased openly so nothing the client said is revealed.

client.project: We've hired an agency to build a customer portal for us, with a defined scope and a fixed budget that we've agreed on. I'm pretty busy, so I mostly want to know it's on track and gets delivered as agreed.

turns.question: What is the one thing you would like to be different for your business once the portal is live?
turns.answer: I'd like our customers to be able to look things up and handle routine requests themselves, instead of phoning or emailing our team for every little thing. That would free up a lot of my staff's time.
turns.rationale: Took the question from the client persona agent. No conflicts are reported, so rule 2 applies: a priority 1 question on a missing topic. The real goal is missing, and both sides describe only a deliverable. Nothing has been asked of the client yet, so this agent is a fair first choice.

turns.question: How would you know, a few months after launch, that customers really are handling things themselves rather than phoning or emailing your team?

turns.rationale: Taken from the client persona agent's priority 1 question. There is no fundamental conflict, only a workable one about change handling, which is a priority 2 matter for this side. The first rule is satisfied, so the next applies: a priority 1 missing topic. The client persona has been asked once, so the two-in-a-row limit is fine. The question builds on the client's own words about phoning and emailing and avoids anything the agency said about small yeses.

No fundamental conflict is confirmed, only workable ones, and the client agent's priority 1 gap (no baseline or date for the success measure) is the most open topic. The client has already given two answers from this agent, so this is the second in a row, which is allowed.

story.title: The scope that was counted every Friday
story.context: An agency builds a new product for a client.

agency.project: We're building a new product for a client with a defined scope and budget. Every Friday we show them a running tally of any changes, and if the total growth goes past ten percent, we stop and check in before going further.

turns.question: In your own words, what is the client really trying to achieve with this new product, and who is it for?
turns.answer: Honestly, I'm working from the agreed scope, which tells me what we're building but not the client's deeper business goals or exactly who the end users are. I'd be guessing if I went further, and it's probably worth confirming with them directly.
turns.rationale: Took the question from the client persona agent. No conflicts are flagged and no agent has been asked yet, so rule 2 applies: a priority 1 question on a missing topic. The real goal and audience are missing for the agency side, and it is the foundation for testing whether both sides picture the same outcome. I kept the wording open and used only words the agency person has said (product, client).

turns.question: How many rounds of changes have you priced for, and what happens once those are used up?
turns.answer: We haven't priced by rounds. What we agreed is budget headroom for approved extras, plus the Friday tally and a check-in once growth passes ten percent. I haven't thought about what happens beyond that if the headroom runs out before we hit the ten percent mark.
turns.rationale: No conflicts exist, so rule 1 does not apply. The client persona has nothing to ask this side and the agency persona has been silent, so rule 3 favours agency or ops, who have both been heard from least. I took the agency persona's priority 1 question on rounds of changes, since the agency side has only just opened up on change and it follows on from the Friday tally. The ops price and exclusions question is next in line.

The agency agent's question was effectively just answered, so I am asking ops' priority 1 question on headroom size, trimmed to one question and avoiding anything the client said about it.

client.project: We've hired an agency to build a new product for us, with a set scope and budget. Every Friday they'll show me a running tally of any changes, and if the total growth goes past ten percent we stop and check in before going further.

turns.question: What's the problem you hope this new product will solve, and what would be different for you once it's finished?
turns.answer: Right now we're patching this together with manual workarounds and spreadsheets, which eats a lot of time and leads to mistakes. Once the product is finished, I'd want it all handled in one place so I'm not spending my week chasing things down.
turns.rationale: No conflicts are reported, so rule 1 does not apply. Rule 2 applies: the client persona agent's priority 1 question on the real goal is missing for this side, and it is the most fundamental gap, since both sides only describe how the work is managed and neither states an outcome. I took that question, keeping it to one part and using only words the client has used (new product).

turns.question: Which specific tasks do the spreadsheets and workarounds cover today, and roughly how much of your week do they take up?
turns.answer: They cover tracking orders and approvals, reconciling numbers between a few different sheets, and sending status updates by email. I'd estimate it eats around a day and a half of my week, and more when something goes wrong and I have to trace the error back.
turns.rationale: No conflicts are reported, so I went to rule 2, a priority 1 missing topic for the client side. Client agent has been asked once, so a second question from it is allowed. I chose the baseline question because the goal is stated as a feeling with no measure, and the client has just mentioned time lost and mistakes, so I'm following that thread.
